Justin Welsh is the most-analyzed creator on LinkedIn. There are probably hundreds of posts, threads, and articles dissecting his methods. Most of them either inflate his techniques into pseudoscientific neuroscience frameworks, or they treat his specific playbook as universally applicable.

Both are wrong, and both do readers a disservice.

What Welsh has actually built is impressive and worth studying. He grew from zero to over 500,000 LinkedIn followers while building a business generating over $10M in revenue with no employees. His newsletter, “The Saturday Solopreneur,” has grown to 200,000+ subscribers. His courses have sold consistently for years. This is a real result built on a real system.

But the system works because of a specific confluence of factors: his starting point (a sales executive background with enterprise-level credibility), his topic selection (solopreneurship, which has enormous aspirational appeal on a platform full of people quietly dissatisfied with employment), his timing, and his willingness to study what works obsessively and iterate fast. Not all of those are replicable.

This analysis looks at what he actually does, why it works, and where the honest limits of applying his approach to your situation are.

## Who Justin Welsh Is, and Why That Context Matters

Before analyzing his content strategy, you need to understand his starting position. Welsh spent years as a Chief Revenue Officer in SaaS, most notably at PatientPop, where he helped scale the company from roughly $1M to $100M in ARR before a successful exit. He left that role after burning out, documented that experience publicly, and built his personal brand around the arc of “burned-out executive goes solo and figures out how to make money without a company behind him.”

That backstory is load-bearing. It gives him instant credibility with two different audiences simultaneously: people in corporate jobs who are dissatisfied (he was one of them), and entrepreneurs who want to understand how to build revenue without a team (he’s done it). He can speak authentically to both because he genuinely lived both.

This matters because a lot of people try to copy his hook style, his post structure, even his vocabulary, without having an equivalent backstory to draw on. The techniques are learnable. The credibility they’re grounded in has to be earned separately.

His LinkedIn profile currently describes him as a “$10M Solopreneur.” That framing is deliberate and effective. It’s specific enough to be credible ($10M, not “built a successful business”), aspirational enough to attract attention, and paired with a term (“solopreneur”) that carries associations of freedom and independence rather than the complexity and risk most people associate with “entrepreneur.”

## The Core of His Content Strategy: One Problem, Repeated Endlessly

The most important thing about Welsh’s content strategy isn’t his hook formulas or his posting schedule. It’s his focus.

He has described his content philosophy this way: solve one expensive problem repeatedly. His answer to “what problem do you solve?” is: how do you build attention or revenue on your own? Every piece of content he creates orbits that question. Posts about mindset, about specific tactics, about his own journey, about solopreneur life, all of them connect back to that core problem. He has published this framing on his [own website](https://www.justinwelsh.me/article/linkedin-strategy), and it’s one of the clearer strategic articulations you’ll find from any creator operating at his scale.

This sounds obvious. It’s extremely rare in practice.

Most LinkedIn creators spread across adjacent topics, dilute their message, and end up building an audience that follows them for entertainment but doesn’t see them as the definitive voice on anything specific. Welsh avoided this by picking a clear positioning and staying inside it. His audience always knows what they’re getting.

The business implication: his LinkedIn audience is pre-qualified for his products. If you follow Welsh, you’re either interested in solopreneurship, personal brand building, or freedom from traditional employment. Those are exactly the people who buy his courses and newsletter. His content and his business are perfectly aligned in a way that doesn’t happen by accident.

For a deeper look at how content strategy and [LinkedIn content monetization](/blog/linkedin-content-monetization) connect, that piece covers the full mechanics.

## His Actual Post Structure: The Trailer, Meat, and CTA Framework

Welsh has shared his content framework publicly. His posts follow a three-part structure:

**The Trailer:** Everything visible before the “…more” cutoff. The trailer’s job is to break the scroll with the first line and make the hook compelling enough to click through. He’s described this clearly: “The first line should break the scroll. The second line should build on it or create tension. The last line before ‘see more’ should promise a payoff worth clicking for.”

**The Meat:** The body of the post, after the click. This delivers on whatever the trailer promised. Welsh’s meat sections tend to be formatted for scanability: short paragraphs, sometimes numbered lists, always with a clear progression toward a conclusion. He avoids dense blocks of text. The pacing is fast.

**The CTA or CTC (Call to Comment):** The closing line. Welsh often ends with a direct question or invitation for the reader to share their experience. This is strategic: comments extend a post’s reach in LinkedIn’s algorithm significantly, and ending with a question is the simplest way to generate them.

This structure isn’t complicated. Most LinkedIn guides teach something similar. What makes Welsh’s execution different is the quality and specificity of each component, particularly the hooks.

## The Hook Patterns That Actually Drive His Engagement

Welsh’s opening lines are the most studied part of his strategy, and for good reason. They’re good. Here are the patterns that appear consistently across his highest-performing content, based on publicly observable posts:

**The contradiction opener.** He states the opposite of what people expect or believe.

- “Confidence isn’t something you find.”
- “The best business advice I ever got was: stop taking business advice.”

These work because they create a momentary cognitive friction. Your brain expects a sentence to confirm what you already believe. When it doesn’t, you read the next line to resolve the tension.

**The direct mirror.** He describes a behavior or internal experience the reader recognizes in themselves, precisely.

- “You like. You save. You lurk.”
- “You watch everyone else win.”

The specificity is what makes these land. Not “many people struggle with taking action” but the exact behaviors: liking posts without commenting, saving content you never revisit, watching other people’s results without starting your own. The reader feels seen. That feeling drives engagement.

**The provocative claim with a data point.** He states something definitive and slightly unexpected, sometimes with a number attached.

- “Someone less experienced is ahead of you.”

These generate comments because some people agree vigorously and some push back. Both responses extend the post’s reach.

**The numbered list opener.** Clean, scannable, promises a discrete amount of value.

- “7 things I wish I knew before I left my $400K job.”

These perform reliably if the subsequent list items actually deliver. Welsh’s do.

What makes his hooks work isn’t a secret formula. It’s precision. He writes about specific experiences in specific language, not general themes in general language. That’s a craft skill, and it improves with iteration.

For the technical side of hook writing and [LinkedIn content strategy](/blog/linkedin-content-strategy), that guide covers the full approach.

## The Link Strategy: What He Does and Why It Works

One of Welsh’s more widely cited tactics is his link-in-post strategy. He publishes posts without external links, lets the post accumulate organic reach during the algorithm’s initial scoring window (roughly the first 2-3 hours), then edits the post to add a business link or CTA afterward.

This works because LinkedIn’s algorithm penalizes posts with external links significantly: posts with links see approximately 60% less reach than equivalent posts without links. By publishing clean content first, Welsh maximizes his initial distribution. Once the algorithm has already distributed the post widely, he adds the commercial element.

The “link in first comment” workaround, which was a popular alternative, is also penalized as of early 2026. Welsh’s edit strategy sidesteps both penalties.

This is one of the genuinely useful tactical specifics from his playbook. It’s replicable, and it makes a measurable difference in reach. The caveat: it requires either manual monitoring to know when to edit, or a disciplined posting workflow. Most people won’t do it consistently.

## The Engagement Investment: 45 Minutes Every Morning

Welsh has shared publicly that he spends approximately 45 minutes each morning responding to comments on his posts. He responds to roughly 75% of the comments he receives.

This isn’t passive. It’s the unsexy part of his system that most people skip when they try to replicate his results.

Comments do two things. They extend the algorithm’s distribution window for a post: each new comment restarts or extends the engagement signal. They also build the relationship between Welsh and his audience at scale. People who get a personal reply from someone with 500,000+ followers remember it. They become more loyal readers. They’re more likely to buy.

The math is demanding. At Welsh’s follower count, a well-performing post might receive hundreds of comments. Responding to 75% of them in 45 minutes requires speed and a degree of templated thinking. Early on, when he had fewer followers, the engagement was proportionally smaller but the discipline was the same.

If you’re building a LinkedIn presence and you’re not engaging with comments in the first hour after posting, you’re leaving reach on the table. The algorithm rewards early engagement velocity. [Growing on LinkedIn fast](/blog/grow-on-linkedin-fast) covers this mechanic in detail.

## His Content Categories: What He Actually Posts About

Looking across Welsh’s publicly visible posts, his content breaks into a fairly consistent set of categories:

The ratio of promotional content to value content is worth noting. Welsh is careful not to oversell. His feed is predominantly giving. When he does promote something, his audience has been conditioned to trust his recommendations because they’ve received consistent value first.

This is a deliberate trust accumulation strategy, and it works. But it requires patience. CEOs and founders who want to immediately convert LinkedIn followers into customers tend to promote too early and too often, which burns the goodwill before it fully accumulates.

## The Vulnerability Ladder: How He Uses Personal Stories Without Losing Credibility

Welsh shares difficult personal experiences publicly. The burnout. The anxiety. The fear of leaving a high-compensation executive role. The failure of early products. He does this in a specific way that builds trust without undermining his authority.

The pattern: he always contextualizes the vulnerability with what he learned and what changed. He doesn’t share struggles for sympathy. He shares them to demonstrate that difficult experiences are navigable, which is directly relevant to an audience considering a risky career or business transition.

A post about burnout ends with “here’s what I changed.” A post about a product that flopped ends with “here’s what it taught me about validation.” The vulnerability is real, but it’s always paired with forward motion.

This works because it matches Welsh’s audience’s actual psychology. His readers aren’t looking for commiseration. They’re looking for evidence that difficult transitions are possible. His personal stories are evidence, not just content.

The practical implication: vulnerability in content works when it’s relevant to your audience’s journey and when it comes with resolution or learning. Vulnerability as a performance, shared without genuine relevance to what your audience is going through, reads as exactly that.

## The 30-for-30 Method: Research and Relationship Building

Welsh has described a customer research practice he calls the 30-for-30 exchange. He identifies people in communities (Reddit, LinkedIn groups, comment threads) who are grappling with the problem his business addresses. He offers 30 minutes of his time to help with their specific problem, in exchange for 30 minutes of them describing their problem in detail.

This is a two-sided value exchange. The person gets genuine help from someone with relevant expertise. Welsh gets deep qualitative insight into how his potential customers describe their own problems, what language they use, what they’ve already tried, what’s frustrating about existing solutions.

The intelligence from these conversations directly shapes his content. When Welsh writes a post that makes readers feel like he’s describing their exact internal experience, it’s partly because he’s done structured research into what that internal experience actually looks and sounds like. He’s not guessing at mirror moments. He’s drawing on real conversations.

This is probably the most underappreciated part of his system. Most creators write about what they think their audience wants to hear. Welsh writes about what he’s heard his audience actually say, in their own words. The difference in resonance is significant.

You can implement a simplified version of this without Welsh’s follower count. Ten conversations with potential audience members or customers will give you more useful content intelligence than a month of analytical guesswork.

## What Doesn’t Transfer Directly: The Honest Limits

Here’s where most Justin Welsh analysis fails to go. There are real limits to how transferable his playbook is.

**The topic has saturated.** The “solopreneur” positioning was genuinely novel when Welsh built his brand around it. It’s considerably more crowded now. If you try to build the same positioning from scratch in 2026, you’re entering a market Welsh helped create, competing against him and the hundreds of creators who’ve followed his model. You need a more specific sub-niche or a genuinely different angle.

**His credibility came from a specific career trajectory.** Welsh’s authority on building attention and revenue online is grounded in having built a $100M ARR SaaS company before going solo. If you haven’t built something significant first, the same content themes feel less earned. The framework is learnable, but the underlying credibility has to be real.

**The engagement investment scales with his system.** Welsh’s 45-minutes-per-day comment response ritual works because his entire business runs on LinkedIn visibility. He has one creator, one newsletter, two courses. His entire workflow can prioritize this. A CEO of a growing company with a team to manage, investors to communicate with, and operations to run cannot realistically make the same investment without trade-offs. Be honest about your available time.

**Mindset content doesn’t work for every audience.** Welsh’s permission-giving and mindset content resonates deeply with his audience because his audience is specifically composed of people who want permission to make a change. If your audience is CFOs, procurement heads, or technical buyers, content about “starting before you’re ready” lands differently. Know whether your audience actually wants mindset content before making it 30% of your feed.

**You can’t separate the content from the product-market fit.** Welsh’s content and his business are unusually well aligned. His LinkedIn audience is his market. The people who follow him for content are the same people who buy his courses. Many CEOs build LinkedIn audiences that don’t overlap well with their actual buyer personas. If your business sells to enterprise procurement teams but your LinkedIn content appeals to startup founders, you’re building the wrong audience.

## The Broader LinkedIn Content Picture: Where Welsh Sits

Welsh is the most visible practitioner of what you could call the “personal brand as business” model on LinkedIn. But understanding him requires understanding where this model sits in the broader LinkedIn ecosystem.

His approach is optimized for a specific business model: digital products (courses, newsletters) sold to a general professional audience interested in independence and income. The tactics that maximize for that business model, specifically the emotional resonance content, the permission-giving, the high comment volume, aren’t necessarily optimal for a B2B SaaS CEO trying to build pipeline, or a management consultant trying to attract enterprise clients, or a healthcare executive trying to build thought leadership.

Different goals require different content postures. A management consultant builds authority through dense, specific insight that signals expertise. An enterprise SaaS CEO builds authority through clear industry perspective and proof of customer success. Welsh builds authority through demonstrated results and relatable personal experience. All three work, but for different audiences and goals.

The mistake is treating Welsh’s specific approach as the LinkedIn playbook rather than one effective approach for one specific context.

For how [LinkedIn works in 2025 and 2026](/blog/linkedin-in-2025) with a broader perspective across business types, that covers the broader picture more completely.

## What You Can Directly Steal From His Approach

Despite the caveats above, there are several things Welsh does that apply almost universally:

**One clear positioning statement.** Know exactly what problem you solve for whom. Say it the same way every time. Your profile, your posts, your bio: all of it should reinforce one coherent idea.

**Specificity in hooks.** Whatever your first line says, make it more specific. Not “leadership is hard” but “I made the wrong hire three years ago and it cost us $400K.” Specificity is what makes content feel real rather than generic.

**Respond to comments in the first hour.** This is mechanics, not optional. The algorithm rewards it. The relationship-building value is real regardless of follower count.

**Publish without links, then add them.** This works. It’s a minor workflow change with meaningful reach implications.

**Study your own data.** Welsh spends significant time understanding what’s working and why. He’s not guessing. Most LinkedIn creators post and check likes. Welsh tracks what drives newsletter signups, what drives DMs, what drives course purchases. Build the same feedback loop.

**Build before you monetize.** He spent months building audience and trust before he had products to sell. The sequence matters. Most creators try to sell too early.

For building the mechanics around a consistent LinkedIn presence, [scheduling LinkedIn posts](/blog/schedule-linkedin-posts) and [LinkedIn automation tools](/blog/linkedin-automation-tools) can help with the operational side once your content strategy is clear.

## The Real Lesson From Justin Welsh

The most honest takeaway from studying Welsh isn’t a hook formula or a post structure. It’s a discipline and a philosophy.

He picked a specific problem. He committed to it publicly. He studied what resonated, iterated quickly, and compounded the results over time. He did the unglamorous work, including the 45 minutes of comment responses every morning, because he understood that consistency of execution is where most people drop out.

And he built a business that’s genuinely aligned with his content, so the effort he puts into LinkedIn has a direct and measurable return. That alignment is something worth engineering deliberately, not something that happens automatically.

If you take one thing from Welsh’s approach and apply it to your own [personal branding on LinkedIn](/blog/personal-branding): get clear on one specific problem, build your content around that problem exclusively, and do the engagement work consistently enough that the compounding can happen. The tactics are learnable. The discipline is the actual differentiator.

For a practical [LinkedIn content strategy](/blog/linkedin-content-strategy) to implement alongside this analysis, that guide covers the operational mechanics. And if you’re building a LinkedIn presence specifically to drive business as a founder or executive, [LinkedIn social selling](/blog/linkedin-social-selling) and [build credibility on LinkedIn](/blog/build-credibility-linkedin) are both worth reading.

Welsh built something real. Study it honestly, take what applies, and ignore the parts that don’t fit your situation.

## FAQ: Justin Welsh’s LinkedIn Strategy

### What is Justin Welsh’s actual follower count on LinkedIn?

Welsh has over 500,000 LinkedIn followers as of mid-2026, with some sources citing numbers approaching 800,000. He has consistently grown this audience since around 2019 through daily posting and deliberate engagement.

### How does Justin Welsh actually make money?

His primary revenue sources are: The LinkedIn Operating System course, The Content Operating System course, The Saturday Solopreneur newsletter (which monetizes through sponsorships at approximately $3,500 per slot, two per week), and occasional consulting or speaking engagements. He has described total business revenue of $10M+ over several years, with margins he has characterized as around 90% due to having no employees and minimal overhead.

### What does Justin Welsh actually post about?

Primarily: solopreneurship and freedom from traditional employment, building attention and revenue as an individual creator, mindset shifts required to leave corporate life, tactical frameworks for content creation and business building, and personal stories from his own transition out of corporate work.

### Is Justin Welsh’s LinkedIn strategy replicable?

The tactics are replicable: his post structure, hook patterns, link strategy, and engagement practices can all be learned and applied. The business model underneath is less universally replicable, because it depends on selling digital products to a large general audience of aspiring solopreneurs, which is a specific market that he has significant first-mover advantage in.

### What is the “link in first comment” strategy and does it still work?

This was a workaround for LinkedIn’s penalty on posts with external links: put the link in the first comment rather than the post itself, to preserve reach. As of early 2026, LinkedIn penalizes this workaround as well. Welsh’s current approach is to publish without any link, accumulate reach, and edit the post to add a link after the initial algorithm scoring window.

### How much time does Justin Welsh spend on LinkedIn daily?

He has described spending 45 minutes each morning responding to comments, plus time for content creation. His total daily LinkedIn investment is probably 60-90 minutes on average. This is manageable for a solopreneur whose entire business runs through LinkedIn visibility, but significant for someone with other operational demands.

### Why do Justin Welsh’s hooks work so well?

The most important reason is specificity. Welsh describes specific behaviors, specific internal experiences, and specific situations rather than general themes. Readers recognize themselves in the specificity. He also benefits from years of iteration: he’s published thousands of posts and has real data on which opening lines drive engagement and which don’t.

### Should I buy Justin Welsh’s LinkedIn course?

The LinkedIn Operating System is well-reviewed and covers his methodology in structured detail. Whether it’s worth the investment depends on whether you’re building the same type of content business he’s built. If you’re a solo creator trying to build an audience to sell digital products to, the framework is directly applicable. If you’re a B2B SaaS CEO trying to drive enterprise pipeline, his system is useful context but not a complete playbook for your situation.

### What does Welsh say about LinkedIn in 2026?

Welsh has written that visuals now dominate the LinkedIn feed and that creators who aren’t using carousels, infographics, or video content are at a disadvantage. He continues to emphasize solving one specific problem repeatedly, consistent posting frequency, and relationship building over virality chasing.

### How does Justin Welsh’s approach differ from other LinkedIn creators?

The main differentiators are: tighter topic focus (he stays inside solopreneurship/personal brand building very consistently), higher emotional resonance in content (he writes to what people feel, not just what they think), and stronger product-audience alignment (his LinkedIn audience and his customers are essentially the same people). Most LinkedIn creators have looser topic focus and weaker alignment between their content audience and their business audience.

### What is the “30-for-30” method Welsh uses?

He identifies people in communities dealing with the problem his business addresses, offers 30 minutes of his expertise to help with their specific situation, and asks for 30 minutes of them educating him about their problem in detail. This gives him structured qualitative research into how his audience describes their own experiences, which directly informs the language and scenarios he uses in his content.

### How do I build a Justin Welsh-style presence without copying him?

Start by identifying the one specific, expensive problem your audience faces that you’re genuinely qualified to help with. Build content exclusively around that problem. Study your own best-performing posts to understand what resonates with your specific audience. Apply Welsh’s structural principles (specific hooks, scannable format, engagement-first) to your own expertise and voice. The framework is the tool; your expertise and perspective are the material.

So I pulled two comparison creators with similar "this actually performs" signals: Marie Robin (smaller audience, same Hero Score) and Alex Banks (similar audience size, slightly lower Hero Score). I wanted to understand what Dan is doing that feels so distinct, and what the others can teach us about different paths to the same outcome.

Here's what stood out:

- Dan writes like every sentence has a cost - and he's not wasting any.
- He turns big, abstract ideas into simple, almost unavoidable claims you want to test on your own life.
- His calls-to-action are quiet but confident, and they consistently point somewhere deeper.

What's interesting is Dan's profile doesn't look like someone trying to "hack" LinkedIn. The connection count is low (253), the cadence is steady (not relentless), and yet the Hero Score is elite. ## What Makes Dan Koe's Content Work

Before we get tactical, I want to call out something subtle: Dan's writing reads like "notes to myself" (which is literally his headline). That framing matters. It gives him permission to be declarative without sounding like he's preaching. You're not being lectured. You're overhearing someone who thinks clearly.

Dan and Alex are closer in audience size, but Dan edges Alex on Hero Score, which hints that Dan's writing mechanics might be creating more "stop and think" moments per impression.

### 1. The "Aphorism First" Hook (and it's not fluff)

The first thing I noticed is Dan often opens with a standalone principle. Not a question. Not a story. A claim.

Stuff like:

- "Nobody remembers those in the middle."
- "The future belongs to the high agency."
- "It is very very easy to repeat the same day for the rest of your life."

These lines work because they force a quick internal reaction. Agree? Disagree? Either way, you're mentally involved. And the tone is sober. No hype. No emoji confetti. Just a clean punch.

Key Insight: Start with a claim that is simple to repeat and hard to ignore.

This works because LinkedIn is a scrolling environment where attention is rented in half-seconds. A short, self-contained line buys you another second. And another.

Dan's posts often imply a fork in the road:

- You're building a distinct path or you're repeating the same day.

Is it perfectly nuanced? Not always. But it creates motion. It makes you pick a side.

A practical way to copy this without being obnoxious is to frame it as consequence:

- "If you can't X, Y won't happen."

Employers won't give you a raise.

That's not random. It's escalation across life domains. It widens relevance without getting vague.

- "Try this:"
- "This goes deeper than you think:"

He develops ideas with minimal steps. No detours. And he often uses a simple progression: diagnosis, consequence, and a bridge to depth.

Dan's CTA psychology is simple: he doesn't ask for commitment, he offers continuation.

- A small bridge line reduces resistance.
- The link being the final line creates a clean stopping point.
- The tone says: "If you're serious, here's more." Not "please validate me."

## FAQ

Q: What is a hook pattern in writing?
A: A hook pattern is the structural move a writer defaults to in the opening one to three sentences of a post, not the topic or the wording. Two posts can share a hook pattern with completely different subjects if the structural move is the same. It is the most-sampled component of voice because the hook is the only part most readers actually read while scrolling.

Q: How does Naval Ravikant open his posts on Twitter?
A: With aphoristic compression: the entire post is the hook and the hook is one sentence, no setup, no qualifier on the first try. Posts stay under fifty words, use present-tense active verbs, and avoid hedging connectors. The compression itself is the voice because it breaks the feed's rhythm before the content registers. The pad is what kills the pattern for imitators.

Q: Why is Sahil Bloom's framework-announcement hook risky to imitate?
A: Because it is one of the AI-drafted defaults in 2026. His move announces a specific framework count up front (three ways, seven mental models) and the body delivers exactly that number. It works because a clear structural promise licenses the reader's attention, but general models default to framework-first hooks too, so a reader who has seen 500 of them this week reads the 501st with suspicion regardless of author.

Q: What makes Paul Graham's hook pattern hard to copy?
A: Paul Graham opens with a blunt claim, then qualifies it in a way that narrows the claim to the version he can actually defend rather than softening it into vagueness. The sharpening is the load-bearing move; the surface structure is just the container. Most imitations get the claim-then-qualification shape right but produce a hedging qualification, which collapses the hook into vagueness.

# What Actually Works on LinkedIn: Lessons From 895 Posts Scored Against Real Engagement

July 10, 2026 · Bradley Jacobs

Mylance is built on this data — see your LinkedIn scored on the levers that actually win:

in/ your-handle

Show me what I should be known for

Almost every "LinkedIn best practice" you have read is someone's opinion dressed up as a rule. Keep it short. End with a question. Post at 8am. We wanted to know which of those rules actually hold up, so instead of guessing, we ran the numbers.

We took 895 real posts from 37 creators in our own database and scored each one against how it actually performed. This is what the data says, including the parts that contradict advice we ourselves used to give. Every finding below is tagged with how much to trust it.

Short version: good content really does beat a creator's own baseline. But polish is a weak predictor. The levers that actually move the needle are specificity, emotional pull, audience-fit, and a few concrete format triggers. The single most overrated trait is being clean, competent, and completely forgettable.

## How we measured it (so you know what to trust)

The trick with LinkedIn "studies" is that big accounts get more of everything, which makes it easy to confuse a large audience with good content. We controlled for that.

- We compared every post only to its own author. A post's score is its engagement (likes, comments, shares) divided by that creator's median post. A 500-follower founder and a 25,000-follower founder are each judged against themselves. "Beat" means a post landed at or above its author's median.
- We used engagement, not impressions. LinkedIn doesn't expose impressions through our integration, so engagement is a proxy. It sits downstream of reach, so suppression and amplification still show up, but pure reach effects are muted. We'll flag where that matters.
- We ran it two ways. First, mechanical features (does the post contain a number, a link, an image) tested against real outcomes. Second, an AI judge scored every post 1 to 5 on quality dimensions, blind to how it performed, and we correlated those scores to reality, with a held-out split so the pattern had to survive on creators the analysis never saw.

Confidence tags: HIGH (held out or replicated), MEDIUM (significant but single-method), DIRECTIONAL (small sample or qualitative). Honest limits are at the end, and they matter.

## The big picture: craft helps, but less than you would hope

Every quality dimension the AI judged correlated positively and significantly with real engagement, and the signal survived the held-out split. So craft is real, not noise. But the effect sizes are modest. A quality score explains only a slice of who wins; the rest is audience-fit, timing, luck, and network effects that live outside the words.

The practical takeaway: treat writing advice as coaching that improves your odds, not a formula that guarantees a hit. Pushing the validated levers reliably makes a post sharper. It doesn't promise a home run. Anyone selling you certainty about LinkedIn is selling.

## What works (ranked by evidence)

### Specificity beats abstraction, every time, HIGH

Posts high on specificity beat their baseline 68% of the time, versus about 50% for vague ones. Named companies, real numbers, concrete detail. "Booked 5 meetings in 2 weeks" beats "drive more pipeline." This one held out cleanly. If you change one thing, make your posts more concrete.

### Emotional pull is the strongest lever we found, HIGH

The cleanest lift in the whole dataset: posts low on emotional pull beat baseline 51% of the time, mid 60%, and high 70%. Vulnerability, stakes, being relatable. Crucially this is a separate axis from how informative a post is. A post can be tactically thin but emotionally rich and still win. Making the reader feel something, or feel seen, isn't a nice-to-have.

### Don't be short, HIGH (and it overturns the usual rule)

This is the finding that surprised us most. Very short posts (under 400 characters) beat baseline only 33% of the time, by far the worst bucket in the study. Everything from 400 characters up sits between 53% and 59%. And long posts do not underperform: posts over 2,000 characters beat baseline 59%, one of the best buckets.

So the popular "keep it short, long-form underperforms" rule is backwards. The real rule is simpler: say enough to be worth reading. Don't post a one-liner and expect it to land. (One caveat resolved below: length only hurts when a long post has no payoff.)

### Add an image, HIGH

Posts with an image beat baseline 61% versus 54% without. A clean, repeatable lift of nearly 8 points. Cheap to do, so do it.

### Put a number or result in the first line, MEDIUM

Posts with a number or dollar figure in the first ~160 characters beat baseline 61% versus 52%. A concrete result up top buys the read. This pairs naturally with specificity.

### The engagement triggers the rubric kept missing, DIRECTIONAL

When we read the posts that beat baseline despite mediocre "quality" scores, nearly every one had at least one of these:

- A personal milestone plus a link ("so I finally built my own site, take a look") that makes the network rally.
- Tagging real people by name, which reliably pulls in engagement from those people.
- An explicit closing question or comment-bait.
- A concrete outcome and a named person in the hook ("helped her book two $15K retainers in 60 days").
- A tactical numbered list ("7 strategies", "4 hacks") with save-and-share value, which won even when the list itself was sloppy.

### The formats that over-index, MEDIUM

Not all post types are equal. Beat rates by archetype:

- Journey / Milestone: 72% (the clear winner)
- Story: 60%
- Confession: 59%
- Contrarian: 57%
- Insight: 55%
- Client story: 55%
- Promotional: 52%
- Question: 50%
- Community: 50%

Personal-arc and emotionally loaded formats beat expertise-dump formats. The lesson isn't "never teach." It's that a lesson wrapped in a real story beats the same lesson delivered as a lecture.

## What doesn't work (ranked by evidence)

### A link in the post body, HIGH

Posts with an external link in the body beat baseline 41% versus 56% for posts without. Even on our engagement proxy, where this effect is muted compared to what it does to reach, links in the body drag performance down hard. Put the link in the first comment. This is the most actionable fix on the list.

### Promotional and hard-CTA framing, MEDIUM

Promo-flagged posts beat baseline 53% versus 56%, and Promotional is the weakest-performing real archetype at 52%. Announcement framing dampens a post even when the underlying story is good. Sell by being useful, not by declaring that you're selling.

### Polished but stakes-free, the most overrated trait, DIRECTIONAL

This was the AI judge's single biggest error: over-crediting clean, well-structured posts that simply don't land. We found 67 posts the judge scored 4 or 5 out of 5 that then performed below half their author's baseline, more than twice the number of underrated winners. The recurring flop patterns:

- Dense jargon essays that read like a whitepaper to an audience of dozens.
- Generic "executive wisdom" with no named person, no number, and nothing at stake.
- Right post, wrong audience, a hyper-specific B2B topic dropped into a general feed. Nobody there cares, so it flops regardless of how well it is written.
- Abstract self-help platitudes.
- Walls of 8 or more hashtags, a tell of reach-chasing that doesn't work.

The uncomfortable lesson: the biggest risk to your writing isn't being sloppy. It's being competent and forgettable.

### "Always end with a question", NOT supported here (open question)

The old rule says a reader-directed close drives engagement. In our data, posts flagged with a reader-close beat baseline 52% versus 56%, mildly negative. Yet qualitatively, explicit comment-bait questions were common among winners. The likely reconciliation: the flag also caught weak, rhetorical closes, and genuinely strong posts often don't need a CTA. We are flagging this as unresolved rather than pretending it is settled. A real question earns its place; a reflexive one doesn't.

## Timing and format, at a glance

- Has an image: 61% vs 54% (HIGH)
- Link in body: 41% vs 56% (HIGH)
- Under 400 characters: 33% (HIGH, the reliable killer)
- Over 2,000 characters: 59% (HIGH, long is fine)
- Number or $ in the hook: 61% vs 52% (MEDIUM)
- Best days (Tue, Thu, Sun): 58 to 62% (DIRECTIONAL, small sample)
- Worst day (Sat): 41% (DIRECTIONAL, small sample)

## The finding nobody wants to hear: craft can't separate two similar posts

Here is the most humbling result. Quality scores predict performance across post types, but are nearly blind within the biggest one. Among 432 "Insight" posts, the correlation between the AI's quality score and actual performance was +0.02, statistically nothing. In other words, we can tell that emotional, specific types of posts win. We largely can't tell a great insight post from a mediocre one by craft alone.

That's why we anchor everything on real outcomes instead of a rubric's self-assessment, and it is why a good LinkedIn tool should coach you toward the validated levers rather than pretend it can score your genius.

## The honest limits (please read these)

A study you can't poke holes in is usually hiding them. Here are ours.

- Engagement is a proxy for reach, not reach itself. The true size of the link penalty and promo suppression is understated here, because we can't see impressions.
- 37 creators, and the corpus leans toward B2B "Insight" posts. Patterns for rare formats (Humor, Confession, Question) rest on small samples.
- This is observational, not causal. These are correlations from history, not a controlled experiment. They tell you where to place your bets, not what will definitely happen.
- The junk filter is leaky. Roughly 1% of posts were gibberish or test data that slipped through, which mildly inflates the headline correlations. A stricter rerun may nudge the modest effect sizes down slightly.

None of this changes the direction of the big findings. It just means you should treat them as strong priors, not laws.

## What this means for your next post

If you want a checklist you can actually use before you hit publish:

1. Be specific. One real number, one named thing, one concrete detail beats a paragraph of abstraction.
2. Make them feel something. A stake, a fear, a win, a moment of being seen. Emotion is the strongest lever we measured.
3. Say enough. Don't post a one-liner. Length isn't the enemy; emptiness is.
4. Lead with a result. A number or outcome in the first line buys the read.
5. Add an image. Nearly a free 8-point lift.
6. Move the link to the comments. The single biggest quick fix.
7. Tell it as a story, not a lecture. Journey and confession formats beat expertise dumps.
8. Kill the polish that hides the point. If there's no named person, no surprising number, and nothing at stake, no amount of clean structure will save it.

Want to see how your own drafts score on these levers? Run one through our free LinkedIn Post Grader, which checks a post against the exact findings above in seconds.

## Where this came from, and where it goes

This isn't theory for us. This evidence is the foundation of how Mylance works: our system is built to push you toward the levers that actually predict performance, specificity and emotional pull, instead of the polish that only looks good. It starts from your real positioning and stories and helps you turn them into posts that sound like you and earn attention, in your own voice.

We are releasing the full report, including the archetype breakdowns and the swipe file of the posts that quietly beat the odds, as a companion to this piece. And we'll refresh these numbers as our dataset grows, so this becomes a living benchmark rather than a one-time snapshot.

Yes, but not the way most advice claims. In our study of 895 posts, very short posts (under 400 characters) were the worst performers, beating their author's baseline only 33% of the time. Long posts (over 2,000 characters) did fine at 59%. The real rule is to say enough to be worth reading, not to keep it short.

In our data, posts with an external link in the body beat their baseline 41% of the time, versus 56% for posts without a link. That's a large penalty even on an engagement proxy, where the effect is muted compared to reach. The fix is simple: put the link in the first comment instead of the post body.

The two strongest, held-out levers in our study were specificity (concrete details, real numbers, named things: 68% beat rate when high) and emotional pull (vulnerability, stakes, relatability: 70% beat rate when high). Polish and clean structure correlated far more weakly. Format matters too: personal Journey and Milestone posts beat baseline 72% of the time.

### What is the best type of post to write on LinkedIn?

These sources cover single‑idea selection, hook design, and systemized workflows more than thread pacing or platform specs; there is no direct source coverage here for Amanda Natividad, Katelyn Bourgoin, or Jay Clouse.

## Key Findings
1) Justin Welsh systemizes LinkedIn posts via rotating post types, varied hook formulas, and a repeatable posting system—“making every post look different” while staying on message [1][8].  
2) Welsh’s own workshop emphasizes deliberate structure and experience design in writing (not just “explaining ideas”), indicating intentional choices about a post’s core idea and reader journey [4].  
3) A named third‑party teardown dissects a specific high‑performing Welsh LinkedIn post (“11K-like”) and extracts the writing framework that made it stand out, providing a concrete example-led blueprint [5].  
4) Dan Koe’s LinkedIn/X approach is minimalist and blunt—few moving parts, no sprawling threads—optimized for a single sharp idea per post [2]; he operationalizes this with an LLM‑driven deconstruction process and uses Twitter/X as a low‑cost validation step before expanding ideas into longer formats [7].  
5) Sahil Bloom’s X opening-line patterns are explicitly decoded in a named practitioner piece that analyzes how his hooks function (beyond just surviving truncation), with transferable patterns for readers to adapt [3].  
6) A 2026 study scoring 895 LinkedIn posts against real engagement argues that many widely repeated “best practices” are unreliable, underscoring the value of evidence‑based structure over generic tips [6].  
7) The provided sources do not document Amanda Natividad, Katelyn Bourgoin, or Jay Clouse’s specific post structures, thread pacing/closing, or platform truncation/character specs with dates; these remain uncovered here [3][6].

## Detail
Justin Welsh (LinkedIn-first; also long‑form)  
- Deciding the single idea: Analyses of Welsh emphasize choosing a clear angle and then selecting from a small rotation of proven post formats to present that angle—he “grew… by rotating through… different kinds of posts,” which keeps execution focused while preventing sameness in the feed [8]. The Autoposting.ai teardown catalogs his “real content patterns, hook formulas, [and] posting system,” reinforcing that the single idea is embedded in a format choice with an appropriate hook, not an improvised riff [1].  
- Opening line beyond truncation: The same analysis highlights hook formulas (not one‑off lines) as part of a system—i.e., the opener’s job is to align with the format and promised outcome, not merely to pass “see more” [1]. Welsh’s own workshop stresses designing an experience, implying the hook sets the narrative or problem‑solving arc the post will deliver, not just a curiosity spike [4].  
- Pacing/closing multi‑post threads: None of the Welsh sources here document thread pacing/closing; the coverage focuses on single‑post formats and hooks [1][4][8].  
- Worked example (named; that succeeded): Pawan Singh’s teardown of a specific Welsh LinkedIn post with “11K‑like” performance extracts the “writing framework that made it stand out,” offering a concrete pattern you can mirror (e.g., how the hook, body, and payoff were arranged) [5].
